title: The Kraken of the Spanish Coast

pages.text: Mr Okine showed his class a photo of a beach in Spain with an enormous, pale, soft shape lying on the sand. “What do you think this is?” “A sea monster!” said Nsiah. “Close,” said Mr Okine. “Sailors used to tell stories of a monster called the kraken. This is a real animal: a giant squid.”
sentences: Mr Okine showed his class a photo of a beach in Spain with an enormous, pale, soft shape lying on the sand.
“What do you think this is?” “A sea monster!” said Nsiah.
“Close,” said Mr Okine.
“Sailors used to tell stories of a monster called the kraken.
This is a real animal: a giant squid.”
pages.alt: A teacher shows a photograph of a giant squid on a beach to a class.

pages.text: On the beach in Cantabria, in northern Spain, the squid was about 9 metres long and weighed about 180 kilograms. Ekuba laid her tape measure along the classroom floor. “That is longer than this classroom!” “Nearly,” said Mr Okine. “And that is only one animal.”
sentences: On the beach in Cantabria, in northern Spain, the squid was about 9 metres long and weighed about 180 kilograms.
Ekuba laid her tape measure along the classroom floor.
“That is longer than this classroom!” “Nearly,” said Mr Okine.
“And that is only one animal.”
pages.alt: A girl measures the classroom floor to compare it with a giant squid.

pages.text: “So why is it a mystery?” asked Ekuba. “Because for most of history,” said Mr Okine, “nobody had seen one alive in its home. They live deep in the ocean, where it is dark and cold. Most of what we knew came from dead animals washed ashore or caught in nets.”
sentences: “So why is it a mystery?” asked Ekuba.
“Because for most of history,” said Mr Okine, “nobody had seen one alive in its home.
They live deep in the ocean, where it is dark and cold.
Most of what we knew came from dead animals washed ashore or caught in nets.”
pages.alt: A diagram shows the deep ocean far below a ship, dark and cold.

pages.text: “In 2012, a team led by a zoologist named Tsunemi Kubodera filmed a giant squid in its natural home for the first time. It was near some islands in Japan. They followed it down to about 900 metres.” “Only in 2012?” said Nsiah. “Yes. Very recently,” said Mr Okine.

They followed it down to about 900 metres.” “Only in 2012?” said Nsiah.
“Yes.
Very recently,” said Mr Okine.
pages.alt: A camera on a small submersible films a squid in the deep ocean.

pages.text: Ekuba listed what scientists know: a giant squid has eight arms and two longer feeding tentacles, a hard beak, and the biggest eyes of any animal. Nsiah drew it. “Why such big eyes?” “Probably to see faint light in the deep,” said Mr Okine. “That is a scientific guess, not a proven fact.”

Nsiah drew it.

“That is a scientific guess, not a proven fact.”
pages.alt: A student draws a giant squid with huge eyes while another writes a list.

pages.text: “What do we still not know?” asked Ekuba. “Many things,” said Mr Okine. “Where they live and travel, how many there are, how long they live, how they find each other, and what they do for most of their lives. Remember: not seen does not mean not real. And seen once does not mean we know everything.”

pages.alt: A board lists questions: where, how many, how long, how.

pages.text: “What about the kraken?” asked Nsiah. “Old stories may have grown from real sightings of giant squid,” said Mr Okine, “but we cannot prove it. Stories often start from something real and then grow.” Nsiah wrote: Kraken stories: maybe a real squid. Big stories get bigger.

pages.alt: A drawing of an old sailing ship with a giant tentacle rising from the sea.

pages.text: At the end, Ekuba stood up. “The mystery of whether giant squid are real is solved,” she said. “The mystery of how they live is still open.” Mr Okine smiled. “That is how most science works,” he said. “One answer, and then ten better questions.” The end.

Scientists keep asking how they live.
